idiom_name: StandardMBean/MXBean in the platform MBeanServer + JMX connector (jconsole)
implementation_notes: The JVM ships a control bus: the platform MBean server. Register each component as a StandardMBean or MXBean (or annotate it with Spring's @ManagedResource) and it becomes remotely reachable through jconsole or a JMX connector, with attributes for status and operations for commands (start, stop, suspend, reload) and notifications for the event half. Because JMX is standard on every JVM deployment it is the default Java realization; the message-based form (Camel's controlbus or a JMS control queue) is justified when the control target is a route rather than an object, or when the console already speaks messaging.
pitfalls: The platform MBean server is local to the JVM by default; remote management needs a JMX connector (RMI/JMXMP) with authentication and TLS, and an open connector is remote control of the whole process.

ObjectName is the addressing scheme: renaming a route or registering two MBeans under one name fails with InstanceAlreadyExistsException, so names belong in configuration alongside the routes they expose.

MBean operations run on the caller's or connector's thread, so a long operation blocks the console and can deadlock with the component's own locks; commands should hand work to the component's loop and report progress through attributes.

variants.name: Apache Camel controlbus component: route lifecycle over a message channel
variants.implementation_notes: In a Camel application the control bus is literally an endpoint: controlbus:route?routeId=X&action=start|stop|suspend|resume|restart|fail|status|stats (or controlbus:language:<lang> for scripting) sends management messages through the same ProducerTemplate/route fabric as payload, with the result returned in the message body (statistics as XML). This is the closest realization of the EIP pattern: management commands travel as messages on channels separate from the business routes, and async=true lets commands run without a reply when the console does not need one. Prefer it inside Camel or Spring Integration systems where route lifecycle - not object state - is what is being controlled.
pitfalls: action=stats depends on JMX being enabled on the CamelContext, so message-based control still drags in the MBean layer for the statistics half.
async=true discards the result: it must never be used for status queries, and even for commands the console loses the acknowledgement that distinguishes applied from ignored.
The control route itself can be stopped by a control message (action=fail/stop), leaving the application with no management path; keep the control endpoint on a route the console cannot suspend.

variants.name: Spring Boot Actuator endpoints (HTTP and JMX) with custom @Endpoint commands
variants.implementation_notes: For Spring Boot services the control bus already exists: Actuator exposes health, metrics, loggers, env, scheduledtasks and shutdown over HTTP (/actuator/**) and JMX, with per-endpoint access levels (management.endpoint.<id>.access), exposure lists and Spring Security integration (EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint() with a dedicated role). Custom commands are @Endpoint classes whose @ReadOperation/@WriteOperation methods are automatically reachable over both technologies, and the same operation therefore serves the HTTP console and JMX tooling. Only /health is exposed by default - the exposure list is the deliberate control-surface decision, and shutdown stays disabled until it is explicitly enabled.
pitfalls: Everything added to management.endpoints.web.exposure.include becomes remotely reachable: an unauthenticated Actuator is a well-known takeover vector, so expose it on a management port and require a role.

Endpoint operations are technology-agnostic and accept only simple parameter types (the docs say so explicitly), so command DTOs must be flattened into parameters or moved to a dedicated @RestController.
The default exposure and access model changes between Spring Boot versions (and shutdown is disabled by default): pin the exposure/access properties explicitly instead of relying on defaults.
